blocks.heading: Using and reviewing the plan
blocks.text: A business plan helps set goals, define the product, identify the consumer, organise research, coordinate marketing and seek finance. It can reveal gaps before money is committed and provide a reference against which actual progress is reviewed. A potential lender can assess the proposal and repayment assumptions, but a plan does not guarantee approval. Managers can assign actions and investigate differences between forecast and actual results. The plan should be updated when evidence changes: a lost customer can affect production, promotion and cash together. Uses are the decisions the document supports; elements are its contents. Explain the link rather than merely repeating a section heading.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tula Repairs plans a new service but a paid trial produces fewer orders than forecast. Use the results to revise demand and resource commitments, then update finance and the action timetable. Ignoring the evidence to preserve the original document would defeat the planning purpose.

blocks.heading: Goals as a planning use
blocks.text: A business plan makes objectives explicit and provides a basis for reviewing progress. A defined result and period help distinguish a successful action from merely being busy. Goals must fit resources and should be revised through evidence rather than adjusted just to conceal failure.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Hena Print targets a reliable small-order service and monitors on-time completion over its first month. The plan provides a standard for review. A large number of leaflets distributed would not by itself prove that the service goal was met.

blocks.heading: Product decisions as a planning use
blocks.text: A plan helps define the product or service and test whether its features meet customer needs within capacity and cost limits. It can reveal that an attractive feature is unaffordable or impractical. The product should fit the wider offer: promised variety affects equipment, inputs and staffing as well as promotion.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tano Bags considers many styles but can reliably produce one durable range. Planning exposes the mismatch and supports a focused feasible launch rather than an unsupported promise of variety.

blocks.heading: Consumer focus as a planning use
blocks.text: A plan identifies who is expected to buy, the need served and how those consumers can be reached. This helps prevent production for an undefined everyone. Consumer interest must include the ability and willingness to pay the feasible price, not merely liking the idea. A narrow target also creates dependence that should be recognised.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Nalu Meals targets nearby workers with short breaks. Its plan can align portability and collection speed with that need. Tourist evening menus would be a different consumer offer requiring separate evidence and capability.

blocks.heading: Research priorities as a planning use
blocks.text: Planning helps identify missing information, choose relevant research and decide what evidence should precede investment. It can prioritise an unknown price response over collecting facts already available. Research has a cost, so link it to a consequential uncertainty rather than gather unrelated statistics. Findings should update the plan when they contradict initial assumptions.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Omi Furniture knows workshop capacity but not whether buyers will pay its proposed price. The next study should test price and demand among suitable buyers. Another description of machinery would not close that market gap.

blocks.heading: Coordinating marketing as a planning use
blocks.text: The plan links marketing actions to objectives, budgets and operational promises. It can prevent a promotion generating orders the business cannot deliver. Product, price, promotion and access should support the same target. Review actual response and cost rather than assume that carrying out an advertisement achieves the objective.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Eya Repairs plans a promotion but has limited appointment capacity. It should coordinate the message and booking limit with available staff, then review completed paid jobs. Advertising unlimited immediate service would conflict with the operation.

blocks.heading: Seeking finance as a planning use
blocks.text: A plan communicates the proposal, funding need, expected return and cash assumptions to potential finance providers. It can help lenders or investors assess risk, while helping owners see whether finance is affordable. It does not create an entitlement to a loan or guarantee that forecasts will occur. State the requested amount and use, supporting evidence and contingencies clearly.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tula Tools seeks a loan for equipment and presents cost, customer evidence and repayment forecasts. The lender can assess whether expected cash supports instalments. A high sales goal without cost or receipt evidence would be less persuasive and does not establish repayment capacity.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Business-plan components and usefulness
blocks.text:
Hela Meals has checked equipment capacity and preparation costs for a small service. Its draft plan includes marketing, production, organisation, finance and an action timetable, but sales rely on the owner’s guess rather than customer evidence. The owner has time for one further investigation before deciding whether to commit.

a Explain how a coherent business plan could reveal the risk in Hela’s proposal. [8]
b Evaluate whether a complete-looking plan is sufficient evidence to commit to the launch. [12]

a Comparing research, marketing, production and finance exposes that the sales figure lacks customer evidence. Capacity and costs support the operational side but not demand. The action plan should schedule the missing investigation before major commitment and assign responsibility. A reviewed plan can therefore reduce inconsistency rather than merely describe intentions. b Having all headings improves organisation but unsupported forecasts can still mislead. Hela has useful capacity evidence and a structured draft, yet expected revenue may fail if buyers reject the price or offering. Seek suitable demand evidence and use a limited trial before a large launch. Finance and implementation should be revisited using the result. A plan supports judgement; its existence alone is not viability proof or a guarantee of funding.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Business-plan components and usefulness
blocks.text:
Ota Bags has a coherent draft plan and verified workshop capacity and costs. Demand at its proposed price remains untested. The owner compares further market investigation with repeating the completed capacity check.

Evaluate Ota’s next investigation. Give a concise plan. [12]

Purpose: use the business plan to identify the largest unresolved risk. Evidence: workshop capacity and costs verified; price demand untested. Market investigation can challenge the revenue assumption and update marketing, production quantities and finance. Repeating a sound capacity check adds less new information at this stage. Judgement: prioritise demand evidence before commitment while retaining all plan components and checking for new changes.
